Let

\[
c=2013,\qquad P_n=y_ny_{n+1}.
\]

From the recurrence,

\[
y_{n+2}=\frac{y_n+2013}{1+y_{n+1}},
\]

so

\[
P_{n+1}=y_{n+1}y_{n+2}
=y_{n+1}\cdot \frac{y_n+2013}{1+y_{n+1}}.
\]

Thus

\[
P_{n+1}
=\frac{y_ny_{n+1}+2013y_{n+1}}{1+y_{n+1}}
=\frac{P_n+2013y_{n+1}}{1+y_{n+1}}.
\]

Subtracting \(2013\),

\[
P_{n+1}-2013
=\frac{P_n-2013}{1+y_{n+1}}.
\]

Now \(y_{n+1}\ge 1\), so \(1+y_{n+1}\ge 2\).

Suppose \(P_1\ne 2013\). Then the nonzero integers

\[
|P_1-2013|,\ |P_2-2013|,\ |P_3-2013|,\dots
\]

form a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, because each term is divided by an integer at least \(2\). That is impossible for an infinite sequence.

Therefore we must have

\[
P_1=y_1y_2=2013.
\]

Then the same relation gives \(P_n=2013\) for every \(n\). Hence for all \(n\),

\[
y_{n+2}
=\frac{y_n+2013}{1+y_{n+1}}
=\frac{y_n+y_ny_{n+1}}{1+y_{n+1}}
=y_n.
\]

So every valid sequence is \(2\)-periodic, with

\[
y_1y_2=2013.
\]

Now factor

\[
2013=3\cdot 11\cdot 61.
\]

The positive divisor pairs \((y_1,y_2)\) with product \(2013\) are

\[
(1,2013),\ (3,671),\ (11,183),\ (33,61).
\]

Their sums are

\[
2014,\ 674,\ 194,\ 94.
\]

The minimum is \(94\), attained for example by \(y_1=33,\ y_2=61\), giving the sequence

\[
33,61,33,61,\dots
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{94}
\]
